metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready badminton records focused only on injury risk, S&C priorities, load management, readiness adjustment, and return-to-court progression across beginner, intermediate, and advanced players. Explicitly preserve badminton-specific exposure channels: lunge volume, smash and overhead stroke volume, jump and landing load, deceleration, tournament density, and tissue-specific risk flags.

key_concepts.concept: Badminton load should be modeled as separate exposure channels: lunge volume and intensity, overhead and smash volume, jump and landing count, acceleration/deceleration density, low stance time, rally density, match/tournament density, gym load, and recovery status.
key_concepts.backend_use: Do not collapse badminton court load into session duration alone. Store load channels separately so a smash-heavy multiball session and a lunge-heavy defensive session can trigger different risk rules.

key_concepts.concept: The smash and the lunge are not merely technical actions; they are high-value exposure markers. Smash volume concentrates overhead, trunk-rotation, elbow, wrist, and landing load, while lunge volume concentrates knee, ankle, Achilles, shin, hip, and back load.
key_concepts.backend_use: Track smashes and lunges as first-class load metrics and link them to tissue-specific plan adjustments.

key_concepts.concept: Lunge count is not enough. Direction, foot orientation, approach speed, fatigue state, skill level, reach distance, stance width, trunk control, and recovery step all alter lower-limb load.
key_concepts.backend_use: When lunge mechanics are flagged as poor, reduce lunge intensity or fatigue density before reducing every badminton session equally.

key_concepts.concept: A scissor-kick recovery jump, jump smash, split-step hop, defensive block jump, and reactive reach landing have different tissue demands. Landing quality and fatigue are as important as jump count.
key_concepts.backend_use: Classify jumps into split_step, jump_smash, scissor_kick, reactive_reach, repeated_hop, and low_amplitude_rally_hop where possible.

key_concepts.concept: Patellar and Achilles tendons need progressive capacity from heavy slow or eccentric/isometric loading plus gradual reintroduction of fast energy-storage loads such as lunges, hops, split-steps, and jump landings.
key_concepts.backend_use: For tendon-sensitive athletes, preserve tolerable strength loading while temporarily reducing high-fast court exposure and checking 24-hour symptom response.

key_concepts.concept: Shoulder, elbow, and wrist symptoms should not be managed only at the joint. Smash and overhead stroke tolerance depends on trunk rotation, scapular control, rotator cuff capacity, thoracic mobility, grip/forearm capacity, timing, and lower-body positioning.
key_concepts.backend_use: Shoulder or elbow flags should retrieve trunk, scapular, rotator-cuff, forearm, and stroke-volume records together.

key_concepts.concept: A player can be globally fresh but locally overloaded at the patellar tendon, Achilles, shoulder, forearm, or low back. Readiness therefore needs whole-athlete markers and region-specific pain or stiffness markers.
key_concepts.backend_use: Combine session RPE, sleep, stress, illness, mood, soreness, and body-region pain/stiffness before assigning court and gym exposure.

key_concepts.concept: Dense tournament periods are not the place to chase new fitness adaptation. They require exposure budgeting, warm-up consistency, post-match downregulation, tissue checks, sleep protection, and tactical choices that reduce unnecessary jumps, lunges, and maximum smashes when possible.
key_concepts.backend_use: When match_count_in_event or matches_per_48h is high, switch plans from overload to readiness, activation, and recovery with only microdosed maintenance.

key_concepts.concept: Beginners need braking, landing, lunge shape, balance, trunk control, basic strength, calf capacity, and shoulder preparation before dense multishuttle lunges, maximal jump smashes, or fatigue drills.
key_concepts.backend_use: Gate beginner court conditioning by movement quality and soreness response, not by ambition or match calendar.

key_concepts.concept: Intermediate players can progress badminton-specific load, but should not spike lunge depth, smash count, jump landing, and match density in the same week.
key_concepts.backend_use: Allow one primary exposure emphasis per week unless the athlete has high training age and green readiness.

key_concepts.concept: Advanced players need high specific capacity, but the risk question becomes whether the current week matches their personal load history, event density, tissue response, and role/discipline demands.
key_concepts.backend_use: Use rolling exposure baselines for smashes, lunges, jumps, sRPE load, and match count, while avoiding universal thresholds detached from individual history.

key_concepts.concept: Return-to-court should progress from pain-controlled capacity to controlled footwork, controlled hitting, integrated rallies, practice participation, match exposure, and finally return to performance.
key_concepts.backend_use: Create staged badminton return records rather than a single cleared/not-cleared flag.

technical_models.name: Badminton Load Accounting Model
technical_models.coaching_translation: A session can be high-risk because it is lunge-heavy, smash-heavy, jump-heavy, deceleration-heavy, or recovery-poor. The backend should preserve the load reason.

technical_models.name: Action To Tissue Stress Map
technical_models.backend_use: Use the action tag to retrieve the correct injury-risk, S&C, and return-to-court records.

technical_models.name: Smash And Overhead Contact Volume Taxonomy

level_implications.beginner: Count only high-intent overheads when formal tracking is not practical; avoid repeated max smashes under fatigue.
level_implications.intermediate: Track max smashes, jump smashes, and multi-shuttle overhead blocks separately from normal rally contacts.
level_implications.advanced: Track total overhead contacts, high-intent contacts, jump overheads, and 24-hour shoulder/elbow/wrist response.

technical_models.name: Lunge Volume And Intensity Taxonomy
technical_models.backend_use: Progress lunge depth, speed, density, and reactivity separately. A high-count low-depth teaching session should not be treated the same as a low-count maximal defensive lunge session.

stage_0_medical_and_symptom_control.goal: Control pain, swelling, irritability, and basic daily function before badminton-specific loading.

stage_1_capacity_rebuild.goal: Restore local strength, mobility, balance, and trunk control without chaotic court demand.
stage_1_capacity_rebuild.court_exposure: basic shadow movement, no maximal lunges, no max smashes, no reactive play

stage_2_controlled_footwork_and_hitting.goal: Reintroduce planned badminton patterns at low to moderate intensity.
court_exposure: limited controlled smashes if shoulder/back tolerant

stage_3_integrated_drills.goal: Blend movement and hitting with moderate reactivity while controlling volume.

stage_4_practice_participation.goal: Return to normal practice with exposure caps and no competition density.

stage_5_match_exposure.goal: Return to competition in managed dose.

stage_6_return_to_performance.goal: Restore pre-injury or target performance load, tournament density, and high-intensity skill execution.
court_exposure: tournament density only after repeat tolerance

technical_models.name: Badminton S&C Priority Stack
technical_models.backend_use: Retrieve foundational S&C before advanced plyometrics when the player lacks strength, balance, trunk, or landing control.

technical_models.name: Beginner Intermediate Advanced Load Progression Model

beginner.court_load: short technical blocks, planned footwork, low-volume lunges, controlled overheads, low-amplitude hops.
beginner.snc: bodyweight strength, balance, trunk control, calf raises, shoulder/scapular basics, landing and braking mechanics.

intermediate.primary_goal: Specific capacity with controlled exposure progression.
intermediate.court_load: tracked lunge and smash blocks, progressive jump landing, moderate multishuttle, planned match play.
intermediate.snc: progressive lower-body strength, unilateral strength, deceleration, lateral power, trunk rotation control, cuff/scapular and forearm work.
avoid: heavy eccentric lower body before match

advanced.primary_goal: High specific tolerance and performance repeatability.
advanced.court_load: individualized smash, lunge, jump, rally, and tournament exposure based on history and readiness.
advanced.snc: strength and power maintenance, microdosed plyometrics, individualized tendon and shoulder durability, high-quality deceleration and reactive work.
avoid: novel soreness-producing gym blocks in competition weeks
high smash multiball on top of shoulder symptoms

tactical_rules.rule: If readiness is yellow, reduce the most relevant exposure channel rather than deleting all badminton. If readiness is red, stop provocative court load and route to clinical review when indicated.
tactical_rules.rationale: Load management is about matching exposure to current capacity and tissue response, not blanket rest or blanket overload.

tactical_rules.rule: High-intent smashes, jump smashes, and repeated multishuttle smashes should be capped or reduced when shoulder, elbow, wrist, low back, or landing symptoms are present, or when the player has a recent overhead-volume spike.
tactical_rules.rationale: Smashes concentrate overhead kinetic-chain and landing stress; multiball practice may not match normal match workload and can create dense repeated exposure.

tactical_rules.rule: Deep, fast, reactive, and fatigued lunge exposure should progress gradually, especially after layoff, growth spurt, ankle sprain, knee pain, Achilles symptoms, shin pain, or back pain.
tactical_rules.rationale: Lunge biomechanics and injury risk are modified by depth, approach speed, fatigue, direction, foot orientation, and skill level.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not add dense plyometrics, jump smashes, or repeated scissor-kick landing blocks unless landing quality is stable and the previous 24-hour tendon, knee, shin, and back response is acceptable.
tactical_rules.rationale: Jump and landing stress can be productive when dosed and coached, but stiff or fatigued landings increase tissue load.

tactical_rules.rule: During tournament weeks or events with three or more matches in a short window, reduce new overload and prioritize activation, warm-up quality, recovery, tissue checks, and exposure budgeting.
tactical_rules.rationale: Dense match exposure, uncertain scheduling, travel, repeated warm-ups, and limited recovery change the goal from adaptation to availability and repeatability.

tactical_rules.rule: The day before a meaningful match should avoid heavy eccentric lower-body loading, dense lunge conditioning, high-volume jump landings, and high-volume max smashes.
tactical_rules.rationale: Badminton performance depends on sharp footwork, shoulder timing, decision speed, and fresh tendons. Fatiguing loads close to competition can degrade quality.

tactical_rules.rule: The day after high match exposure should start with region-specific checks: ankle stability, knee/tendon response, shin pain, Achilles stiffness, shoulder/elbow/wrist soreness, and low-back symptoms.
tactical_rules.rationale: Delayed symptom response is central for tendons and bone stress, and match exposure can be highly individual.

tactical_rules.rule: When growth-spurt or adolescent maturation flags are present, avoid adult-like spikes in plyometrics, deep lunges, max smashes, match density, and heavy loading. Keep strength technique, balance, trunk control, mobility, and recovery habits high priority.
tactical_rules.rationale: Youth athletes require maturation-sensitive programming and can be vulnerable when sport-specific load rises faster than tissue capacity.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not move from pain-controlled rehab directly to full match play. Return must pass controlled footwork, controlled hitting, integrated reactive drills, full practice tolerance, and limited match exposure.
tactical_rules.rationale: Return-to-sport is a continuum; badminton requires restoration of tissue tolerance, movement quality, reaction, timing, confidence, and competition density.

tactical_rules.rule: Sharp pain, swelling, giving way, suspected rupture, neurological symptoms, night pain, worsening shin focal bony pain, or pain that changes gait or stroke mechanics should stop progression and trigger medical review.
tactical_rules.rationale: These features may indicate injuries that are not appropriate for normal load modification alone.

tactical_rules.rule: Complex plyometrics and reactive deceleration drills should be layered on top of adequate lower-body strength, calf capacity, balance, and landing skill, not used as a substitute for them.
tactical_rules.rationale: Plyometrics can improve power and agility, but poor tissue capacity and landing control can turn useful elastic work into excessive joint and tendon load.

physical_demands.name: Lower-Body Strength Capacity
physical_demands.description: Badminton requires repeated split-steps, accelerations, decelerations, lunges, jump takeoffs, and landings. Squat, hinge, step-down, split-squat, calf, and hip strength support both performance and load tolerance.

priority_by_level.beginner: high - bodyweight and light external load with technical control
priority_by_level.intermediate: high - progressive bilateral and unilateral loading
priority_by_level.advanced: high - individualized strength maintenance or development around competition

physical_demands.name: Lunge Absorption And Push-Off
physical_demands.description: Players must brake into deep positions, absorb impact, control knee/ankle/trunk alignment, strike or defend, and push off rapidly without losing balance.

physical_demands.name: Deceleration And Reacceleration
physical_demands.description: Badminton repeatedly asks players to stop, redirect, and accelerate from unstable or stretched positions, often with little time between actions.
programming_notes: Progress speed before density only when alignment is stable.
Pair with trunk and hip strength so the knee and ankle are not absorbing all load.

physical_demands.name: Jump And Landing Load
physical_demands.description: Split-steps, repeated hops, scissor-kick jumps, net kills, and jump smashes create recurring ankle, Achilles, knee, hip, and back load.

physical_demands.name: Shoulder, Scapular, And Rotator Cuff Capacity
physical_demands.description: Overhead strokes and smashes require repeated shoulder rotation, scapular control, trunk contribution, and fatigue-resistant external rotation capacity.

physical_demands.name: Elbow, Wrist, And Forearm Capacity
physical_demands.description: Repeated gripping, rapid pronation/supination, net kills, drives, late hits, and high-intent smashes can overload wrist and elbow tendons when stroke volume or grip tension spikes.

physical_demands.name: Trunk Rotation And Spine Capacity
physical_demands.description: The trunk transfers force between lower body and racket during smashes and controls posture during lunges, low stances, late overheads, and recovery steps.

physical_demands.name: Calf, Soleus, Foot, And Ankle Capacity
physical_demands.description: Badminton demands repeated elastic split-steps, forefoot loading, lunges, rapid push-offs, and landing absorption, making calf-soleus and ankle capacity central to performance and risk control.

physical_demands.name: Repeat Rally Conditioning
physical_demands.description: Players need to repeat short high-intensity rallies with fast recovery while preserving lunge quality, overhead timing, decision quality, and landing mechanics.
programming_notes: Conditioning should not be so fatiguing that lunge or landing mechanics degrade for large volumes.
Use aerobic support away from dense match periods when recovery is poor.
Multishuttle conditioning should be counted as both conditioning and skill-load exposure.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Ankle Sprain From Lunge, Split-Step, Or Landing
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Fast lunges, unstable foot orientation, split-step hops, jump landings, change-of-direction, or landing on an opponent/partner foot can create inversion, eversion, or instability episodes.
prevention_or_management: Use balance and proprioception work.
Restore calf, peroneal, and foot strength.
Progress lunges from planned to reactive.
Use PAASS-style criteria for return after acute sprain.
Consider brace or taping decisions with a clinician for recurrent sprain history.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Knee Pain, Patellofemoral Load, And Patellar Tendon Overload
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated lunges, braking, low stances, jump landings, and rapid direction changes increase knee extensor and patellofemoral demand, especially when hip/calf strength or landing mechanics are insufficient.
prevention_or_management: Track lunges, jumps, and next-day response.
Use progressive heavy slow, isometric, or strength loading when appropriate.
Reduce high-fast jumping and deep fatigued lunges during reactive symptom phases.
Progress energy-storage work before full return to match density.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Achilles Tendon Overload Or Rupture Risk
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated split-steps, forefoot push-offs, scissor-kick landings, jump smashes, and rapid accelerations load the Achilles tendon heavily. Sudden spikes or deconditioned return increase concern.
prevention_or_management: Build calf and soleus capacity progressively.
Use eccentric or heavy slow loading as clinically appropriate.
Progress hops and jump landings gradually.
Treat sudden rupture signs as urgent medical referral.
Use 24- to 72-hour tendon response to guide high-fast load.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Shin Pain, Medial Tibial Stress, And Bone-Stress Risk
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated impact from split-steps, hops, running drills, jumping, hard braking, and sudden increases in court volume can irritate the tibial stress complex.
prevention_or_management: Reduce impact and hop density early.
Maintain fitness with lower-impact conditioning when needed.
Build calf, soleus, foot, hip, and trunk capacity.
Progress return to hopping and court load only when symptoms are stable.
Refer when pain is focal, worsening, or stress fracture is suspected.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Shoulder Overhead And Smash Overload
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Repeated overhead strokes, smashes, jump smashes, late contacts, poor scapular control, limited shoulder rotation, and insufficient trunk contribution can overload rotator cuff and shoulder structures.
prevention_or_management: Track overhead and max smash volume.
Build rotator cuff external rotation and scapular control.
Train trunk rotation and balance.
Avoid sudden multi-shuttle smash spikes.
Use criteria-based staged overhead return after injury.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Elbow Tendinopathy And Grip-Stroke Overload
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: High volumes of gripping, late contact, repeated drives, smashes, backhands, and wrist-dominant strokes can overload lateral or medial elbow tendons.
prevention_or_management: Reduce high-intent and late-contact stroke volume.
Build wrist extensor/flexor and pronation/supination capacity.
Address shoulder, trunk, and timing deficits.
Avoid sudden equipment changes during high-load phases.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Wrist And Forearm Overload
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Fast racket-head actions, net kills, drives, deceptive holds, late defensive contacts, and repeated pronation/supination can overload wrist and forearm tissues.
prevention_or_management: Track high-speed wrist actions when symptomatic.
Use progressive forearm and grip endurance work.
Improve kinetic-chain contribution so the wrist is not the sole power source.
Reduce painful stroke types temporarily.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Low Back Extension, Rotation, And Lunge Compensation Overload
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Smashes, late overheads, round-the-head actions, repeated low stances, deep lunges, and poor hip/trunk control can overload the lumbar region through extension, rotation, side bend, or fatigue compensation.
prevention_or_management: Build trunk anti-rotation and anti-extension capacity.
Improve hip and thoracic mobility.
Reduce late overhead and max-smash density when symptomatic.
Progress lunge depth and court coverage without compensation.
Refer for neurological symptoms or persistent/worsening pain.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Tournament Density And Repeated Match Exposure Risk
injury_or_load_risks.mechanism: Multiple matches in short windows create repeated warm-ups, high arousal, variable rest, travel, sleep disruption, and compressed lunge, smash, jump, and deceleration exposure.
prevention_or_management: Switch to tournament-mode microcycles.
Use activation and mobility rather than overload.
Budget smashes, lunges, and jumps.
Use post-match recovery and tissue checks.
Avoid extra conditioning during dense events.

training_implications.recommendation: Build movement literacy and tissue capacity before badminton-specific fatigue. Teach landing, braking, split-step rhythm, controlled lunges, shoulder preparation, trunk control, and calf capacity with low soreness.

Introduce specific capacity while controlling exposure spikes. Track lunge, smash, jump, and match density; add progressive lower-body strength, trunk/scapular work, calf capacity, deceleration, and planned plyometrics.

Individualize exposure using load history and performance goals. Maintain high strength and power, microdose plyometrics in-season, track tissue-specific response, and protect freshness during tournament blocks.

Use plyometrics as high-quality, low-to-moderate volume power work, not conditioning punishment. Begin with landing and low-amplitude elastic contacts, then progress to lateral, horizontal, rotational, and reactive contacts.
Train braking as a skill before using shuttle runs as fatigue conditioning. Athletes should own trunk position, hip-knee-ankle flexion, foot pressure, and recovery step before reactive or dense work.

Treat smash durability as kinetic-chain capacity. Include thoracic mobility, trunk rotation power/control, scapular control, cuff strength, horizontal pulling, forearm capacity, and volume-managed overhead exposure.

When patellar or Achilles tendon symptoms are present, reduce high-fast court loads first while preserving clinically appropriate slow strength. Use pain and 24-hour response to decide whether to progress, maintain, or regress.

Tournament weeks should prioritize repeatability and availability. Training should become activation, mobility, light technical rhythm, scouting or tactical rehearsal with controlled physical load, and recovery.

Return-to-court plans should stage individual exposure channels. A player may be ready for controlled clears before max smashes, shadow footwork before deep reactive lunges, and practice before tournament density.
